Coach Reyes had assigned Ethan his first eight hundred metre race on Saturday, and Ethan wanted it badly, because the winner of the city meet got to carry the team banner at the season parade. The problem was the distance itself. His watch said he always started fast, died halfway, and finished crawling.

Marcus waved him over between shots. "You know it's only two laps, right? Four hundred metre track, so the eight hundred is exactly two laps. Everybody plans it as a first lap and a second lap."

"Two laps," Ethan repeated. "That's all?" He had assumed it was some enormous distance, and now a new worry replaced the old one. If the race was only two laps, then the thing that separated winners from losers was invisible. Nobody could see energy being saved or spent. He would have to deduce it from numbers, from the way his legs felt at each mark, like a detective working with clues he could not watch directly.

He decided on an experiment. He did a time trial, and at the halfway line he counted the runners scattered around the loop, a quick census of who was ahead and who was behind, and matched it against where his own legs were burning. He tried again the next evening, holding back on purpose through the whole first lap even though it felt embarrassingly slow, then letting everything go on the second. His total time dropped by six seconds. Same legs, same track, different plan. He grinned at Marcus, who was dribbling with one hand and watching with the other.

On race day, the starter's gun cracked and twenty boys surged forward. Ethan stayed near the back, and the crowd at the far turn began shouting at the leaders, voices rising as runners stretched out. Rounding into the home straight, the boy beside him, wearing an eccentric mismatched pair of shoes, one red and one green, suddenly sprinted as if the finish had come. Ethan's own legs screamed at him to follow. For three strides he almost did, because everyone was yelling and the finish line flag was right there, snapping in the wind. Then his experiment spoke louder than the crowd. One lap down. One to go.

The red-and-green shoe boy crossed the line, slowed, and staggered when he realized nobody else had stopped. Ethan passed him on the backstretch of the second lap, breathing in rhythm, and poured out everything he had saved as the flag came around again. He lunged across the line second, and Marcus was already vaulting the railing, shouting, "That's my cousin!"

Annabelle crouched at the top of the skate park's shallow bowl with a marble, a stopwatch, and a clipboard, because Mr. Ruiz had said their graphs were due tomorrow and hers was still blank. She had tried measuring the marble in the school hallway, but kids kept walking through, and her graph had come out a mess of dots that jumped around like flies. Here, on the smooth concrete of the bowl's rim, nobody would bother her.

"Whatcha doing?" A boy on a skateboard rolled up beside her, one wheel squeaking. His name was Dev, and he'd been circling the park all afternoon, waiting for his turn on the big ramp.

"Timing a ball," Annabelle said. "Ten centimeters, twenty, thirty. I write down how long it takes to reach each mark, then I plot it."

Dev scratched his chin. "You can draw a picture of speed?"

"That's the weird part. You can't see speed. You only see where the ball is and what the clock says. The graph is how you catch it." She let the marble go and clicked the stopwatch as it crossed each chalk mark. "Five seconds. Almost the same again. Almost the same again."

Dev sat down on his board, forgetting the ramp entirely. "It's slowing down, though, right? Everything slows down. My grandpa says his pension slows down every year, whatever that means. Money stuff."

"The marble loses a little speed, sure. But look." She plotted her points on the clipboard: ten centimeters at five seconds, twenty at ten, thirty at fifteen. When she connected them with her ruler, they fell along one clean line, slanting up from the corner like a hill. "It's straight."

"So?"

"So I thought the line would curve. A ball that's slowing should bend the line, shouldn't it?" She stared at it. The floor was so smooth, so polished by ten years of skateboards, that the marble barely lost anything at all. She dropped her pencil and grabbed the marble again. "Okay, one more run to justify this. If it's real, it'll do it twice."

She rolled the marble down the far side of the bowl, where the concrete was rougher and scattered with pebbles. This time the dots scattered, and the line she could draw through them bent and drooped. She held both graphs side by side.

"Dev, look. A straight sloping line means the ball is going at a constant speed. This one's straight, so it's constant. This one bends, so it isn't."

Dev picked up the marble and squinted through it at the sun. "So on the smooth floor, the ball never changes its mind."

"Something like that," Annabelle said. She checked her watch and yelped, because the park closed at six and her graph still needed labels. She flipped to a clean page and started the axes, and Dev, still holding her marble hostage, said, "Do the rough floor one more time. I want to watch it bend."

Eleanor had the whole evening planned: roast chicken, a big green salad, and her grandmother's lemon cake. Her parents were both working late, and she wanted dinner ready when they walked in the door. She'd already trimmed the raw chicken and set it in the oven pan, and now she pulled the lettuce from the fridge and reached for the cutting board on the counter, the one still slick from the chicken.

She stopped with the knife in her hand. Something her science teacher had said in the fall came back to her, something about bacteria hopping from one food to another. It even had a name. "Cross-contamination," she said out loud, trying the word. The lettuce was going into the salad raw. Nobody would cook it, and cooking was what made the chicken safe in the first place. The lettuce would go straight from board to bowl to mouths, exactly as it was.

She rinsed the knife, washed her hands, and slid the used board into the sink. Then she pulled the plastic-wrapped clean board from the cabinet, the one she used for bread, and set it on the counter beside the salad bowl. Outside the window the sky had turned an ominous gray, and fat drops of precipitation spattered the glass. If it kept up, her dad would come home soaked, which meant she should put towels by the front door too. She added it to her mental list while she tore the lettuce into pieces.

Her little brother Marcus wandered in, sniffing the air. "Is that cake?" He pointed at the lemon zesting setup next to the stove.

"Cake comes after dinner," Eleanor said. "Want a job? Wash these tomatoes." She handed him three and elaborated on the plan, since Marcus always worked better when he knew the whole shape of it. "Salad first, then chicken comes out, then we ice the cake while everything's hot on plates."

"What's this board for?" Marcus asked, picking up the second one from the sink.

"That one had raw chicken on it," Eleanor said. "It has to be washed with soap before anything else touches it."

Marcus made a face and set it down like it might bite him. "That's why you got the other one out?"

"Exactly." She dried her hands and checked the oven. Through the little window the chicken was already turning golden at the edges.

When their parents came in, shaking rain off their coats, the salad was sitting crisp and cold on the table, and Marcus was carrying the lemon cake with both hands like a trophy. Their mother paused at the counter, taking in the clean board, the soapy one in the rack, the two of them standing there.

"You used different boards," she said.

Eleanor smiled and lifted the carving knife. "Dinner in ten minutes."

Luca had carried four bean plants into the gymnasium in a cardboard box, and now he stood beside his folding table arranging them in a row. Three of the plants had grown tall under his grow light at home, but one was small and pale. That one was his favorite, even though kids walking past kept frowning at it.

"Your plant's dying," said Marcus, leaning over the table. "That's going to embarrass you when the judges come."

"That one's the one that got only plain water," Luca said. "The other three got the fertilizer. It's my control group."

Marcus looked blank, so Luca pointed at each pot in turn. "This one got fertilizer once a week. This one got it twice. This one got it every day. And the control group gets no change at all, no fertilizer, just water. That way I can compare everything against it." The plain-water plant had barely grown, while the once-a-week plant had shot up taller than the others. The every-day plant had yellow leaves that looked almost endangered, drooping at the tips. Luca wrote a note on his chart about it.

During the fair, a judge in a green sweater stopped at Luca's table. She asked what the small plant was for, and Luca explained his rows and his chart, showing how the once-a-week plant had grown the most while the plain-water plant gave him the starting point to measure from. The judge asked what he would do differently next time, and Luca said he would test more plants in each group, because one bean plant alone could just be a weird bean plant. The judge smiled at that and made a mark on her clipboard.

After she moved on, Marcus came back with his own project, a volcano that had fizzled twice before working. "I just dumped baking soda in all my test cups," he admitted. "I didn't have anything to compare against."

"You could run it again," Luca said. "Set one cup aside with nothing in it at all. My mom says the second try is where the real science happens." He slid his chart across the table so Marcus could see the rows.

Marcus studied it, then jogged off toward the supply table where the extra cups were stacked. "I'm redoing it before the next judge comes around!" he called back.

Luca turned his plain-water plant so its label faced the aisle, right beside the tall one.

Victor stood at the microphone in the school gymnasium with his hands jammed in his pockets, waiting for the word he was sure would end his run at the county spelling bee. Across the bleachers sat his little sister, holding the flashcards he had made her carry on the bus even though she complained the whole way.

"Bite," the pronouncer said. "B-I-T-E. The silent e does nothing. This language is a mess," Victor whispered, because the pronouncer had already called time on the word before, when Victor had stopped mid-spell to grumble about it, and the judges had agreed to postpone his turn until the end of the round rather than mark him out.

From the bleachers his sister shouted, "Mrs. Okoye called it the Great Vowel Shift!" Victor's face went hot, but the judges only chuckled, and the pronouncer nodded. "That's true," she said. "Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed after spellings had started to become fixed." She tapped her cards. "It's a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation. Now spell the word, please."

Victor had planned to argue that the whole system was rigged, that memorizing was like being frugal with the wrong currency, saving up letters that bought nothing. But something clicked instead. If the vowels had shifted while the letters stayed frozen, then the e in bite wasn't a trick. It was a fossil, proof of an older sound. He tested the idea quickly, silently. "Meet" must once have rhymed with "mate." "Bite" with "beet." The pattern held, at least for the words in his stack of flashcards, which he had drilled like a frontiersman chopping through a wall of vowels nobody had warned him about. Spelling wasn't random. It was archaeology.

"B-I-T-E," he said. "Bite." The bell stayed silent, and the pronouncer smiled and gave the next speller a word, and Victor walked back to the folding chair in the line of surviving contestants. His sister gave him two thumbs up. He had come in believing the bee was pure memorization, a contest of brute repetition, and now he wasn't so sure. There was a system underneath, buried but real, and he wanted to dig for it.

He slid the flashcards out of his back pocket and, on the bus ride home, turned them over one by one, hunting for fossils. When he found "name," he tapped the card against the window and said, "You too, huh."

Blake had one hundred eighty-two dollars in his desk drawer, and he wanted it to be more. It sat under a model rocket kit he had never built, and every so often he counted it, which changed nothing.

At dinner his sister Priya, who was sixteen and annoyingly good with money, mentioned that her savings account earned six percent interest. Blake slid his oatmeal-raisin cookies toward her until she agreed to explain. Simple interest, she said, paid you the same dollars every year, six dollars on every hundred, over and over. She drew it on a napkin: a flat line of identical payments, five years, thirty dollars on a hundred. Then she said the magic word, compound, and drew the line bending upward, because with compound interest you earned interest on your interest. Blake squinted at the napkin until the numbers blurred.

"Both are six percent," he said slowly, "but one of them keeps feeding itself."

Priya shrugged, which was how she confessed she had already known this for two years and never told him.

That night he sat at the kitchen table with a calculator, graph paper, and the last of the milk. He worked out five years both ways. Simple gave a hundred dollars thirty more dollars. Compound gave more than that, and the difference was small, which disappointed him until he noticed the gap between the lines growing wider each year, like two runners where one kept speeding up. He could not see the interest itself, nothing you could hold, but the pattern on his paper proved something invisible was happening. He tested it backward, too: he started with the compound total and peeled off six percent five times, and landed back near a hundred, close enough that the little difference had to be the interest on interest stacking up.

"How long until my money doubles?" he asked Priya from the doorway.

"Rule of seventy-two," she called back, halfway asleep. "Divide seventy-two by the yearly percentage rate."

He did the math on his hand. Seventy-two divided by six was twelve years. Twelve years at six percent, so his two hundred birthday checks would become four hundred by the time he was twenty-five. He wrote the number on the napkin and taped it inside his desk drawer, right on top of the rocket kit.

The next morning he found the drawer open and forty dollars missing, replaced by a note in Priya's handwriting: "Loan. Compound interest applies. Six percent, payable in cookies."

Blake counted what remained, then counted it again. "Twelve years to double," he muttered, "but about two weeks to get even." He headed for the kitchen to bake.

The highway unrolled ahead of them like a ribbon left in the sun, and George had the whole back seat to himself, which almost made up for nine hours of driving. His science teacher had handed out a packet before spring break: rainfall and temperature graphs for two places, one a rainforest station beside an estuary on the coast, the other a stretch of desert they were, at this very moment, driving through. George's assignment was to compare the climates. His dad had promised they'd stop at the visitor center outside town, and George wanted to be ready, because his older sister Kayla had made a bet with him back in February. She'd said he couldn't figure out what made a desert a desert. He'd said deserts were hot, obviously. She'd grinned in that infuriating way and told him to look it up.

He looked it up now, phone balanced on his knee while saguaro cactuses slid past the window, their arms raised like people hailing a bus. Less than about 250 millimeters of rain a year. He said it out loud, then again, quieter. Ten inches. He pulled out the rainfall graph for the rainforest station and traced the bars with one finger, month after month, some of them taller than his thumb. Then he checked the temperature line, which never dropped below warm. When he flipped to the desert graph, the bars were stubs, hardly bumps at all, though the temperature line swung wildly between baking days and shivering nights.

"A desert is a place that gets less than about 250 millimeters of rain a year," he said to Kayla. "Ten inches. That's the rule."

"So what?" she said, not looking up from her music.

"So it doesn't say anything about temperature. It only says rain." He tapped the packet. "Which means a cold place could count too. A snowy place, even."

Kayla pulled out one earbud. "No way."

"Way. If it gets less than ten inches of precipitation, it's a desert, even if it snows." He remembered, suddenly, choosing his answer back in February, blurting out "hot" without thinking, and he could still feel how dumb it had seemed later, lying awake in his bunk bed. He'd wanted to guess fast instead of guessing right. He wasn't sure yet whether the bet counted as won, since he'd been wrong first, and Kayla would absolutely argue that it didn't.

At the visitor center, a wall map showed rainfall totals painted in bands of color, and George stood in front of it while a lizard watched him from a rock outside the glass. He found a gray stretch far to the south, marked with snowflake symbols, and below it a number: 180 millimeters. Kayla leaned in beside him, silent for a long moment.

"Okay," she said at last. "Half a win."

Grandpa Ray arrived on Sunday with one suitcase, a crossword book, and a plastic box with seven little lids in a row. "That's my pill organizer," he said, setting it on the kitchen counter. "One compartment for every day of the week."

Cameron had planned to show him the tree fort first thing, but by Tuesday morning the fort was still a secret. Grandpa Ray kept asking the same questions. Was it hot out? Was the sprinkler broken? Had anyone seen his reading glasses, which were on top of his head? Cameron felt a small, hot resentment building, the kind you get when a guest rearranges your whole house without touching anything.

On Thursday morning, Grandpa Ray stood at the counter holding his water glass, frowning at the pill box. "Did I take my morning pills?" he asked. "I can't remember. If I take them twice, I'll be in trouble, and if I skip them, that's trouble too." He looked at Cameron the way kids look at teachers when they don't know the answer.

Cameron stepped up beside him. He looked at the box, at the letters printed above each little lid, S M T W T F S. The Thursday lid was open and the compartment under it was empty. He thought about it for a second. Grandpa filled the whole box every Sunday night, Cameron had watched him do it. If the Thursday compartment was empty, and Grandpa always filled them all, then the Thursday pills were already gone. Which meant they were already taken. "You took them," Cameron said. "Thursday's compartment is empty."

Grandpa Ray peered at the box, then laughed so hard he had to set down the water glass. "A detective in the family."

Cameron felt the back fence radiate heat where the sun hit it, and the grass had gone arid and crackly in patches, so he dragged the hose around and turned the sprinkler on. Grandpa Ray sat in a folding chair watching, and when Cameron came out of the sprinkler soaked, Grandpa said, "Tomorrow, check the box for me again, will you? I like the way you solve things."

Friday morning Cameron got to the kitchen first, proud of his job. He lifted the Saturday lid, and that compartment was empty too. For a moment he thought Grandpa had taken Saturday's pills two days early. Then he looked closer and spotted a single white pill lying on the floor under the counter, and beside the box, a spilled strip of pills Grandpa must have been restacking. Cameron picked up the pill and set it in the Saturday compartment. "Grandpa," he called toward the hallway, "I found where Saturday went. You dropped him. He's back home now."

Dinner was tacos, and Tyler had exactly one goal: finish fast so he could get back to his model bridge. His older sister Maya had other plans. She was home from college for the weekend and had brought her psych textbook to the table, which Mom pretended not to notice.

"So we learned this thing in class," Maya said, spooning salsa onto her plate. "It's called the Sally-Anne test. It was first used in 1985. You show a kid a story where Sally puts her marble in a basket and leaves, and Anne moves it to a box while she's gone. Then you ask where Sally will look." She glanced across the table at Zoe, their four-year-old cousin, who was methodically dismantling a taco. "Children from about age four usually say she'll look where she left the marble, in the basket. Zoe's exactly the right age. Can I try it?"

"Maya, let the child eat," Mom said, but she was smiling, and Zoe had already looked up at the word marble.

Tyler opposed the whole idea. Zoe wasn't some lab experiment, and anyway she was sharp. She could count to thirty and knew every dinosaur in her book. "She'll get it right," he said. "I bet you five dollars."

"You're on," Maya said. She took a real marble out of her pocket, which Tyler found suspicious, and set two cups on the table, a blue one and a red one. "Zoe, this is Sally's marble. Sally puts it in the blue cup." She dropped it in. "Now Sally goes outside to play." Maya turned her chair dramatically. "While she's away, naughty Anne moves it to the red cup." She moved it. "Sally comes back. Where will Sally look for her marble?"

Zoe pointed a bean-smeared finger at the red cup. "Right there. She can see it."

Maya raised her eyebrows at Tyler, who felt his ears go hot. "She's four," he said. "Ask her again."

They asked again with a gummy bear and a napkin, and again Zoe chose the place where the thing actually was, not where Sally had left it. Tyler slid the five dollars across the table, but Maya pushed it back. "Keep it. You can run your own census later. Ask every four-year-old you know."

After dinner Tyler found Zoe in the living room, building a tower from the durable wooden blocks that had survived three cousins. He sat down across from her. He didn't run a test. Instead he hid a block under his own leg while she watched him watch the tower, then said, "Zoe, I put a block somewhere. Where will you look?"

She giggled and lifted his elbow, finding it instantly, because of course she knew where it was. She had seen him.

Then she hid her eyes with both hands, put a block behind her back, and said, "Tyler, where's the block? You don't know!" She peeked through her fingers, delighted that he didn't, that she alone held the secret.

So she did know there was such a thing as not knowing. It just worked one way so far. Tyler turned that over while she stacked the next block. Maybe it was like his bridge: you couldn't see the load moving through the beams, but you could test where it went.

"Zoe," he said, "want to see a trick with the marble?" She held out her hand.

Cole's little sister had dumped three different liquids into unlabeled jars last Saturday, and Mom had banned all kitchen experiments until Cole figured out which jar was which. "Vinegar, soapy water, and plain water," Mom had said, sliding the jars across the counter. "If you can prove which is which, you get the counter back." That was how Cole ended up standing in the kitchen on a rainy afternoon with a package of litmus paper, a notebook, and his heart beating faster than it should have.

He had learned the system in science class last week. Acids turned blue litmus paper red, and bases turned red litmus paper blue, and neutral things left both strips alone. Somewhere in between there was a whole scale, from zero at the acid end to fourteen at the base end, and a neutral thing sat right in the middle at seven. The trick was that you could not see acidity itself. It had no color, no smell you could trust. You could only see what it did to the paper, and reason backward, like tracking a laser beam you could not look at directly by the spot where it landed.

He dipped a blue strip into jar one. The paper sat there, blue as ever. He held his breath and counted to ten, but nothing changed. He dropped a red strip into jar two and watched it flush pink, slow and certain, spreading up the paper like sunrise. Into jar three went another blue strip, and it turned red so fast he almost missed it.

"Jar three is the acid," he said out loud, writing fast. "Vinegar. Jar two is basic, the soapy water. So jar one is plain water." He tested jar one with red paper too, and both strips stayed their own colors. Neutral. Proven. He felt like a detective closing a case.

His grandfather was at the sink rinsing a coffee cup, and Cole noticed him eyeing the pink and blue strips. "You know where they get that paper from?" Grandpa asked, pointing his cup at the window. "Those crusty growths on my garden wall out there. Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the things growing on rocks and tree bark."

Cole leaned over the sink and looked out at the gray-green patches crusted across the stones. All this time he had thought they were just dirt. He had been scrubbing past them in vain every summer, complaining about the mess, and they had been quietly making the very paper in his hand. He tore off a fresh strip, held it up to the window, and compared it to the wall.

"Grandpa," he said, "I need a bucket of water. We're scraping some lichen off that wall, and I'm testing the rain barrel."

The word "Rashomon" was on the board when Abigail walked into third period, and Mr. Okafor was already saying something about witnesses. She slid into her seat, still thinking about the mess at home. The vase, the one Grandma Lu brought from her trip years ago, lay in pieces on the kitchen counter this morning like evidence at a trial.

"I want you to try an experiment," Mr. Okafor said. "But first, has anyone actually seen the film?" Silence. He nodded. "Then let's build it from the ground up." Abigail raised her hand before she knew why. "Rashomon," she said. "Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film. It tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other." She had read the back of the DVD case at her uncle's apartment once, months ago, and the sentence had stuck like a burr.

Mr. Okafor asked the class to imagine a broken vase and describe how it broke. Dexter said a cat knocked it. Priya said a strong draft from an open window. Marcus suggested an earthquake tremor nobody else felt. Every version sounded plausible, and Abigail noticed something strange: the more details a speaker added, the more certain the class sounded when they voted. Priya got eleven votes. Dexter got nine. Marcus, who had emphasized the rattling windows with both hands, got six.

Abigail's hand shot up again. Last night, before anyone knew the vase was broken, she had heard her little brother Ben tiptoeing past her door at ten, way past his bedtime. This morning she had heard four versions of the story at her own table. Dad blamed the cat, though the cat had been shut in the laundry room. Ben swore he was asleep. Mom said the vase must have slid off the shelf, which made no sense because the shelf was level. Grandma Lu just said vases break, which was true but not helpful.

"Here's my test," Abigail said, her voice steadier than she felt. "If everyone honestly believes their own version, then the votes tell us nothing about what happened. So I checked one thing. The window was closed all night, and there was no cat loose, and no tremor. That leaves exactly one candidate." She looked around the room. "My brother. He was awake. I heard him."

After class, Mr. Okafor stopped her at the door. "So was it the brother?" Abigail thought of the note she'd found tucked under the vase pieces when she got home, in Ben's terrible handwriting: I was getting water and I caught it but not really. I'll pay for it with my birthday money. She had folded the note small and put it in her pocket, next to the tally she'd made of the family votes.

"Yes," she said. "But here's the weird part. Everybody wasn't lying, and everybody was wrong." Mr. Okafor smiled and held up the DVD case. "Want to borrow it?"

Charlotte slid into her chair at the kitchen table so fast her sock skidded on the tile, and the small white box landed in front of her with a thump that knocked over the salt shaker. "Dad. Dad. Is this it?"

"It's it," her father said, grinning, his hands still damp from washing the dinner dishes. "Fourteen years old. Officially phone age, according to you."

"According to everybody at school," Charlotte said, already peeling the tape. The box opened like a treasure chest, and there it was: a phone, hers, finally hers. She held it up and the screen glowed, and she felt like she had just been handed the keys to a city.

She was typing in her first contact, her friend Priya, when her little brother Marcus wandered in with a granola bar. He leaned over her shoulder like a suspicious inspector checking plumbing. "How long have people even had these?" he asked through a mouthful of oats. "Like, ten years?"

"Way longer," Charlotte said, but then she stopped. Was it way longer? She tried to picture it. She had seen old movies where people made calls from boxes on street corners, so phones had to be pocket-sized only after that. "I think it started in the seventies," she said slowly. "I'm going to look it up. On my phone. That's what it's for, right?" She typed the question and read, and then she laughed out loud. "Marcus, you're wrong and you're going to love this. The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by a Motorola engineer, Martin Cooper, on a New York street, on April 3, 1973. He called somebody while standing on a sidewalk. In 1973!"

"That's older than Mom," Marcus said, awed.

"Rude," their father called from the sink, "but factually I'll allow it."

Charlotte set the phone down flat on the table and looked at it with new respect, as if it were a museum piece that could also show cat videos. She imagined Martin Cooper on that street, holding a brick-sized phone, probably feeling exactly like she did right now. "Okay, first responsible decision," she announced. "Screen time. I'm setting a limit before Mom makes one for me, because if she makes it, it'll be terrible and involve charts."

Her father came over, drying his hands. "Smart. What's the limit?"

"Two hours on school days." She typed it in, then hesitated. "One and a half. If I set my own, I get to brag about my self-control, which is like a bonus hour of enjoyment." The kitchen had gone tranquil, just the hum of the fridge and the tick of the oven cooling, and Marcus quietly stole a second granola bar while everyone was distracted by the glow of the screen.

Then the phone buzzed in her hand, its first buzz ever, and she nearly dropped it. "It's Priya. Already. How does she even know?"

"I texted her mom," her father admitted. "Go on. Answer it. That's what it's for."

Charlotte's thumb hovered over the keyboard, and then she typed her very first message from her very own phone: "Guess who called somebody on a New York street in 1973 before you did."

Chase stood in his great-uncle Ezra's study for the third Sunday in a row, and his bar mitzvah portion still had a hole in it. He could recite the first four verses fine, but verse five kept collapsing on him halfway through, like a bridge with missing planks. Uncle Ezra unrolled the Torah scroll across the long table and weighted its corners with small velvet bags.

"Read along with me," Uncle Ezra said, and began to chant.

Chase leaned close. The Hebrew letters were strange and beautiful, and without thinking he stretched out his hand and lowered one finger toward the parchment, following the line the way he did with his school books.

Uncle Ezra stopped chanting. Instead of scolding, he reached into a wooden box and held out a slim rod with a hand shape at the tip, silver and cool when Chase took it. "A yad," Uncle Ezra said. "In Hebrew the word means hand."

"So the pointer is called hand, because it's like a finger that touches for me?" Chase asked.

"Follow the words with it," was all Uncle Ezra said.

Chase set the tip of the yad under the first word and chanted. The pointer made him slow down. He could not race ahead the way he did from memory, because his eyes had to stay where the silver hand was. When he reached verse five, his mouth wanted to jump to the wrong ending again, but the yad sat under the actual word on the parchment, stubborn and still, and he read what was really there instead of what his memory portrayed. The verse came out whole.

"Again," said Uncle Ezra.

They went around five times. On the last pass, Chase closed his eyes and tried it blind, and the verse held. He opened one eye. "It worked. Why?"

He thought about it while Uncle Ezra rolled the scroll closed. It was like the pointer had trained his brain, some gradual rewiring, neuron by neuron, until the correct path was the easy one. Maybe that was true for piano scales too, or free throws. Did every hard thing get easier if something forced you to slow down first? He wondered whether he could invent a yad for his math homework.

"Next week, no scroll," Uncle Ezra said. "Just you and the words."

Chase twirled the silver pointer once and handed it back. "Next week, I might not need it."

Uncle Ezra smiled and closed the wooden box with a soft click.

Madison wanted to win the school's photo contest more than she wanted lunch, and lunch that day was pizza. The rules were simple: post a selfie somewhere in town, and the picture with the most likes by Friday would take the prize, a new tablet. On Wednesday she had the perfect shot, herself grinning on her front porch with the sunset behind her, and she pulled it up on a lab computer before class to upload it.

Devon leaned over from the next seat. "You're going to post that? Everybody can see your house number."

"No they can't. It's tiny." But she zoomed in anyway, and there it was, sharp as anything: the brass 4 and the crooked 7 nailed beside the door. She zoomed further and spotted the street sign at the corner, Parkview Road, and then the edge of her own school's logo on her brother's backpack hanging on the railing. She sat back. Any stranger scrolling through the feed could put those three things together and work out exactly where the picture was taken, which meant exactly where she lived.

She needed proof, not just a feeling. So she tested it. She pulled up a photo posted that morning by a girl from another school, a girl she had never met, and zoomed in on the background the way she had zoomed into her own. A café menu board. A bus stop number. A gymnasium sign with the name of a middle school across town. In four minutes, using nothing but the picture, Madison had found the street, and from the street she found the girl's actual front steps on a map site. Her stomach went cold, a small corrosive fear that the whole contest was not what it looked like. "That was too easy," she said out loud.

Devon watched her do it. "Okay, that's creepy."

"It's not magic. It's just a mechanism, like a lock. The details are the tumblers." She deleted her upload before it went anywhere. Then she thought about how to fix it instead of giving up, because she still wanted that tablet. She walked home, took the same porch selfie again from a different angle, cropped out the street sign, turned so the house number sat behind her in a blur, and hung the backpack inside. One small change could transform the whole picture from an address into just a sunset.

On Friday the likes poured in, and Madison won. As she carried the tablet out of the lab, Devon held up his phone and grinned. "Nice win. Too bad you posted the winner from the computer lab. That's our school's name on the wall behind you."

"Everyone already knows where my school is," Madison said, and then stopped, one foot in the doorway, because she had just remembered the contest rules printed on the tablet entry form: winner's photo displayed in the lobby, with full name and grade.

Katherine sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with a laptop balanced on her knees, staring at a grid of empty boxes. They had decided to run a lemonade stand together for one last summer before Priya's family moved away in September, and now they had a week of sales scribbled in a notebook: Monday fourteen dollars, Tuesday nine, Wednesday a soggy page with a smudged seventeen. Priya wanted to know if they'd earned enough to split for the fair on Saturday, but adding by hand felt like punishment.

"Type the days in column A," Priya said, "and the money in column B." Katherine did it, row by row, B2 through B10, even the rainy Thursday when they only sold three cups. Then she clicked on an empty cell below the numbers and wondered how to make the machine do the math. She typed =B2+B3+B4 and kept going, but it felt wrong, like listing every friend's name instead of just saying "everybody."

Priya leaned over. "My cousin does this. She says the colon between two cells marks a range." Katherine typed =SUM(B2:B10) and pressed enter. The answer appeared instantly: ninety-one dollars. She changed Wednesday's smudged seventeen to a thirteen, and the total dropped to eighty-seven, which let her verify that the formula really was reading every cell and not just some of them. It was like the grid had a hidden rule, and she had found the thread of it.

"Now the chart," Priya said. Katherine highlighted the days and the numbers, clicked insert, chose bar chart, and there it was: Saturday's bar towered over everything, while rainy Thursday was a stubby little block. The pattern was obvious now in a way it had never been in the notebook. Saturday was unanimous, no argument possible, their best day, and Priya said that next summer, wherever she was, she'd track her own stand the same way.

Then Katherine noticed something. B10 was Thursday, but B11 was empty, and the formula only reached B10. If they sold anything Friday, it wouldn't be counted unless she stretched the range to B11. She fixed it, tested it by typing a five into Friday's spot, and watched the total climb to ninety-two. She deleted the five, saving Friday for Friday.

"Eighty-seven to split," Priya said, "forty-three for you, forty-four for me, because the cups were mine." Katherine agreed, but the chart glowed on the screen between them, week finished, summer almost finished too. "Save the file under my name too," she said. Priya copied it to a flash drive shaped like a strawberry and held it out. "First one to make a chart in their new town wins."

Brielle slid into her seat in the computer lab and typed her name into the login box before the projector had even finished warming up. The assignment was on the board: write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. She had until the end of class to submit it, and the winner of the speed test, Mr. Okoye had promised, would get to pick the theme for the game-design unit. Brielle wanted that pick more than she wanted lunch, and she had skipped half of lunch already to sketch her plan on a napkin.

Her first version worked in ten minutes. It asked for a number, then tried dividing it by every number from two up to the number itself, one at a time, checking for a remainder of zero. Nine worked. Seventeen worked. Then her friend Marcus leaned over from the next machine and typed 1000003 into her prompt. The cursor blinked. And blinked. The little spinner appeared, and the whole lab groaned, because her program had frozen the shared network drive along with it.

"That's going to cost you the speed test," Marcus said, grinning.

Brielle refused to close the window. She leaned close to the screen as if staring could magnify the problem, as if the loop would become visible and confess. "It's testing every single divisor," she muttered. "Nobody needs to test a million of them. There has to be a rule hiding in there." She grabbed her napkin and wrote the numbers out in a column. Fourteen: divisible by two and seven. Fifteen: three and five. Twenty-one: three and seven. Every composite number she wrote had at least one odd divisor. She circled the column twice.

"Okay," she said out loud, not caring that Marcus's colleague at the next station, Priya, had turned to listen. "Once I've checked whether a number is divisible by two, I can skip every even divisor. An odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one." She said it fast, like she was afraid it would evaporate. Then she changed one line so the loop jumped by two instead of one, testing only odd divisors after the check for two, and hit run.

The cursor blinked once. PRIME, printed the screen, for 1000003, faster than she could snap her fingers. Priya clapped. Marcus tried 1000033 on his own machine and watched his version stall while Brielle's answered in a heartbeat.

Then Mr. Okoye walked over, checked the submission list, and raised an eyebrow. "Brielle, your program was first, so you pick the theme. But I should tell you, there's a twist. The game-design unit isn't for this class. It's for the robotics club, and they build whatever the winner designs."

Brielle looked at Marcus, then at Priya, then at the blinking cursor. "Robots," she said. "I pick robots that race."

Kate sat cross-legged in the desk chair, the kitchen smell of onions drifting down the hall while she stared at the blank email. Her thirteenth birthday party was in ten days, and she wanted to invite her whole class, all twenty-six of them, to the skating rink. The problem was that her friend Priya had got upset last month when a class group email showed everyone's addresses to everyone else, and a boy had used Priya's address to sign her up for jokes she hated. Kate's mother had said only one rule governs the family computer, which was to think before you send, and Kate was thinking hard.

She typed the invitation slowly, describing the rink, the time, and the pizza afterward. Then she paused at the row of empty boxes near the top: To, CC, and a third one she had never really looked at, BCC. The letters seemed like a code left there for people who already knew the secret. She moved the cursor over them and read the small words that appeared when she hovered, and she read them twice.

"Blind carbon copy," she said out loud to the empty room. The desk lamp hummed, and the cursor blinked as if waiting. So if she put every address in that hidden field, each person would still receive the message, but the other recipients could not see their addresses. She turned the idea over the way she turned a puzzle piece. If she used the To field, twenty-six people would see twenty-six addresses, including Priya's. If she used BCC, nobody would see anybody's. She needed a way to test it before she trusted it.

Kate sent a practice email to her own address and to her cousin's, placing her cousin in the BCC field. Then she opened the copy that arrived in her own inbox and searched the header for her cousin's name. It was not there. The To line showed only her own address. She heard her mother chopping something in the kitchen, a steady, calm sound, and Kate felt her shoulders come down from around her ears.

She pasted the class list into the BCC field, checked the invitation one last time, and wrote a subject line that sounded friendly but not wild, since a birthday invitation, unlike a hereditary title, did not have to be passed along to everyone a person had ever met. She pressed send. The screen showed the message flying off, and a reply from Priya appeared within a minute: "I'm coming! And thanks for not sharing my address with the whole world." Kate grinned and reached for her skates by the door.

Emily wanted one thing from Tuesday's lab: a graph with points that actually landed in a line. Her lab partner, Devon, had gotten a neat diagonal on his distance-time graph last period, and he had taped it to the front of his binder like a trophy. Emily's plan was to roll a marble across the lab bench, time it with a stopwatch, measure the distance, and calculate the speed. Simple. Except her first timing came out as "about a second, ish," which would not impress anyone.

The trouble was that the marble crossed the bench in less time than her thumb needed to react. She tried again. "Zero point... something," she said, staring at the stopwatch, which seemed pleased with itself. Devon leaned over from the next station.

"You could just guess," he offered. "Guessing is basically data."

"It is not." Emily tapped the stopwatch against the bench. She could see the ball's path clearly, fifteen centimeters at a time, marked with tape. What she couldn't see was the speed itself. It was hidden inside the distance and the time, and her job was to drag it out, to quantify it, using numbers instead of "ish."

Then she remembered the science museum from sixth grade. There had been a long, gentle ramp there, and a sign explaining that the whole thing copied Galileo, who had studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps because the ramps slowed the motion enough for him to time it with the tools of his day. She had stood there for ten minutes letting balls roll while her class moved on to the gift shop. Now she looked at the stack of books at the end of the lab, and the long wooden ramp meant for the friction experiment nobody ever did, still listed on the supply sheet as equipment that was technically not obsolete.

She propped the ramp on two textbooks, aimed it down the aisle past the fern that had been the lab's only surviving organism since September, and marked off distances with tape. "You're the timer," she told Devon, handing him the stopwatch. He shrugged, which was his version of enthusiasm.

The ball took nearly four seconds to travel the first stretch of the ramp. Four whole seconds, long enough to see coming, long enough for even Devon's thumb. They ran it five times, and Emily wrote each measurement in her table, then plotted the points on graph paper. They fell into a line so straight she checked twice for trickery.

"Mine's steeper," Devon said, holding up his trophy graph from the earlier period, his flat-bench speed line rising sharply compared to hers.

"That's the point," Emily said. She rolled the ball again, watched it creep down the gentle slope, and started toward the teacher's desk to ask whether a slower speed could count as extra credit.

Jonathan had taped the last poster board in place when Priya appeared at his elbow, holding a bottle of lemon juice like it was evidence in a trial.

"Your chart says my entry is wrong," she said. "The judges already marked pH 3 on my sheet, and you told Marcus my vinegar is only a tiny bit more acidic than yours at pH 4. That's what the scale says. Three is one number away from four."

"It's one number away," Jonathan said, "but it's not a tiny bit."

Around them the gym hummed with folding tables, baking soda volcanoes, and the eccentric solar-powered carousel that Mr. Ruiz wheeled in every year, its tiny horses spinning in lopsided circles. Jonathan's own display sat between Priya's juice samples and Marcus's tray of mystery liquids: a row of cups, a package of litmus paper, and a hand-drawn pH scale from 0 to 14 with red on one end and blue on the other.

"Prove it," Priya said.

He dipped a strip of litmus paper into her lemon juice and laid it on a paper towel. Red. He dipped another into his vinegar. Red again, but when he held the two strips side by side, the lemon juice strip had turned a deeper, angrier shade. He wrote both numbers on his chart, then stood there staring at the strips, because color alone was not going to settle anything with Priya.

So he tried a different route. He lined up ten cups. Into the first he poured a splash of his vinegar, pH 4. Into each cup after that he added more and more water, diluting it down step by step, and he tested every cup with a fresh strip, writing the pH on masking tape stuck to the side. The numbers climbed one at a time, 5, 6, 7, and Priya leaned in, frowning.

"You watered it down a ton," she said, "and the number only moved by three."

"That's the point," Jonathan said. "It takes that much water just to get from four to seven. Every step up means ten times less acid, so going down one step means ten times more. Your juice at pH 3 isn't a little more acidic than my vinegar at pH 4. It's ten times more acidic. To water your lemon juice down to where my vinegar is, I'd need to dilute it by ten."

Priya picked up his chart, her eyes moving down the tape labels. "You tested it like an algorithm," she said. "Same steps every cup, one thing changing each time."

"I had to evaluate it somehow," Jonathan said. "You weren't going to take my word."

She set the chart down, picked up the lemon juice bottle, and walked straight toward the judges' table, calling over her shoulder, "Then they need to hear this from you, not from me. Come on, and bring your cups."

Jonathan grabbed the tape marker and hurried after her.

Sofia spread her worksheet on the library table and read the question again: find one example of foreshadowing in "The Most Dangerous Game" and explain what it suggests. She had read the story twice, and both times she had sped through the first page the way she sped through the first page of everything, hunting for action. Now she needed the part she usually skipped.

Across the table, Marcus was copying definitions out of a literature textbook. He wanted an A on Monday's quiz badly enough to come to the library on a Saturday, and he kept saying so. "Foreshadowing," he muttered. "When the author hints at what's coming. There. Now symbolism." He wrote it down without looking up.

Sofia turned back to the opening paragraphs. The narrator mentioned sailors' strange dread of a certain island, and then she found the name in the text: Ship-Trap Island. She read it three times. Sailors feared the place before anything had happened there, at least anything the reader had seen yet. She pulled a index card from her backpack and wrote a question at the top: does the name itself warn us? Below it she listed what she knew: the story was about a man who hunted other men, and the island was where he did it. The name, she wrote, sounds like a trap for ships, which is exactly what it turns out to be.

She tested the idea out loud, because that was how she checked things. "Ship-Trap Island," she said. "Nobody on the yacht takes the name seriously, but the sailors do. They're afraid of the place before the story even starts."

Marcus put his pen down. "Say that again." She repeated it. He pulled his own copy of the story over and found the page. "So the fear is foreshadowing," he said slowly, "and the name is basically a warning sign the characters sail right past."

"That's what I've got." Sofia filled in the worksheet, then went back to the second part of the question, symbolism. In the story the yacht lost its rudder, and that detail had seemed random until now. She thought about it, wrote that the broken rudder meant the ship was no longer in control of where it was headed, then crossed out the sentence because it wandered. She wrote a shorter one.

At the front desk, the afternoon sun came through the tall windows and made the dust in the air glow. A boy at the next table tried three times to stack his books into a tower and gave up. Sofia packed her bag, and Marcus held the door.

"Monday, when she asks for examples," he said, "I'm raising my hand first."

"Beat you to it," Sofia said, and walked out into the parking lot before he could argue.

Naomi sat cross-legged in the window seat with the photocopy of Macbeth spread across her knees, and the paraphrase was due at eight. Her group had split the scene into speeches, and hers was the hardest one, the one where Lady Macbeth says the witches' greeting "hath" sent her somewhere strange. She had no idea what that meant. She read the line out loud twice, then wrote underneath it, "The greeting has sent me," and crossed it out, because that made no sense either.

She tried a different approach. She circled every word ending in -eth or -th in her speech. There were five: "hath," "doth," "knows not what he doth," "peradventure," no, that one didn't fit the pattern, so she uncircled it. Then she made two columns on the back of a homework sheet. In the first column she wrote "hath." In the second column she wrote "have" and "has," because it could be either. For "doth" she wrote "does." Her idea was this: maybe the ending was the clue, and if she swapped each old word for its plain twin, the speech would turn into modern English on its own.

She read the line again with her swaps in place. "The greeting hath sent me" became "the greeting has sent me." That worked. "What he doth" became "what he does." That worked too. She felt her pencil speed up, and she scribbled the whole paraphrase in fifteen minutes: Lady Macbeth saying the witches' news has made her dizzy with hope, that she has thought of something robust enough to hold her ambition, something like a treaty between her will and her husband's weakness.

At 7:52 the group call started, and Priya was already panicking about her own speech. "I can't do this one, it's all these weird words, like 'doth,' what even is 'doth'?"

"Doth means does," Naomi said. "And hath means has. They end in -th, that's the trick. Watch." She read Priya's line as printed, then read it again with her swaps, and Priya went quiet on the screen for a second, then started circling words on her own copy, pen squeaking against the paper.

"Okay, okay, I see it," Priya said. "Mine has like nine of them."

"Exactly," Naomi said. "Use every single one." She held her paraphrased speech up to the camera, and on the screen Priya did the same, and between them the two sheets of paper almost touched.

Clara's spreadsheet was supposed to settle an argument. The sixth grade was planning a bake sale, and Room 12 claimed their poster idea would raise more money than Room 11's candy jars. Ms. Okafor had said that whichever room could show the better plan, with real numbers, would get the table by the front door. So Clara built a spreadsheet with a column of prices, typed "=SUM(B2:B9)" in the total cell, and clicked the button for a bar chart to show which items brought in the most.

The total came out to eighteen dollars. Clara stared at it. The eight items on her list were two, three, two, five, three, two, four, and four dollars, and that was not eighteen. She checked her formula twice, then dragged the mouse over the range again to make sure it covered every row. It did. She pressed Enter and got eighteen again.

Marcus leaned over from the next computer. "Just write it in by hand," he said. "Twenty-five. Done."

"No. The computer is skipping something, and I want to know what." Clara looked at the column row by row. Seven of the cells sat snug against the right edge of the column. One, the five, sat against the left edge, over by the wall of the cell, the way words did. She clicked on it. In the formula bar it looked the same as always, a plain five. She clicked a right-aligned cell. Also a plain five. Same digit, different side.

She had a guess: the total was wrong by exactly five, and the five was the odd one out, so whatever made that cell different might be what made the total miss it. To test it, she typed the number five fresh into a blank cell, copied her SUM range to include it, and the total jumped to twenty-three. She deleted the old left-aligned five, retyped it in the same spot, and the total moved to twenty-five. Marcus, watching, said, "So the number was text. It just looked like a number."

"Then SUM skips cells that hold text," Clara said. "It left it out and never said anything." She remembered where the five had come from: she had pasted it from a note the class treasurer had sent, and pasted things could arrive as text. It was a quiet kind of fracture in the data, invisible unless you knew to look at which side of the cell a number sat on.

She fixed the chart, printed the sheet, and taped it to the bake-sale sign-up poster by the door. The bar for chocolate chip cookies stood tallest, and at the bottom, in small letters, she wrote, "Total: $25. Verified twice." Marcus read it and did not resign his candy-jar idea; he just crossed out his own total and wrote, "Ask Clara."

Ms. Okafor stopped at the poster on her way past. "Which room gets the front table?" Marcus asked her.

She tapped the bar chart with one finger. "The one with the math that adds up."

The cast had been on for three weeks, and Vincent still caught himself reaching for the soccer ball with his left arm before he remembered. He sat on the bench at the edge of the field, watching his team run drills, the whistle shrieking every few minutes like a bird that had given up on being subtle. Tryouts for the travel squad were in nine days. Nine days, and his arm was still wrapped in fiberglass like a rolled newspaper.

He kept going back to that day in his head. Coach had warned them about the wet patch near the goal, and Vincent had gone for the aggressive slide anyway, because Dylan had done one first and the whole team had cheered. He had landed wrong, and he had heard the sound before he felt it, a dry branch snapping somewhere inside his wrist. His mother had driven him to the clinic with the radio off, which was how he knew she was scared.

At the clinic, the doctor had turned the X-ray toward the light and studied it for a long moment. "Good news," she had said. "The break missed the growth plate." Vincent had asked why that was good news, and she had pointed at the image. Near the ends of long bones there were growth plates, she said, made of cartilage, and that was where bones lengthened during childhood. A break through one of those could affect how the bone grows. He had looked at the pale line of his own wrist bone and thought about how it was quietly building itself, invisible, and how close he had come to wrecking the machinery.

Now he tested it. He pressed his thumb gently along the cast near his wrist, then farther up his forearm, comparing what he felt. The doctor had drawn an arrow on the fiberglass at the spot where the break was, and he had memorized where the ends of the bone were supposed to be. He pressed near the arrow, then an inch past it, mapping his own arm like a burglar casing a house. It was not science exactly, but the swelling had gone down in a ring around the arrow mark, and the aching had shrunk to a smaller territory every day. He reasoned that the healing was tracking the break, and the break had stayed away from the end of the bone, so the part of him that made his arm longer was safe.

Dylan jogged over, sweating, and flopped onto the bench beside him. "You going to make tryouts?"

"Cast comes off in eight days," Vincent said. "Tryouts are in nine."

"That's cutting it close. What if the arm's weak?"

"Then it's weak for one day." Vincent flexed his fingers inside the cast, all five of them, and watched them answer. His mother thought he should wait a full season, and maybe she was right, and maybe sliding after Dylan that day had been a trade he would still be paying for years from now, in ways nobody could see on any X-ray. He hadn't decided yet.

Dylan held out a water bottle, and Vincent took it with his good hand, then switched it deliberately to the left, gripping until the plastic creaked.

Brooke sat cross-legged on the living room rug with her laptop open on the coffee table, and on the screen was the mess of two hundred and forty survey answers from the whole school. Her little brother's question, "What's your favorite school lunch?", had gone viral, and now she had promised him a real report by dinner. She had figured out pivot tables that afternoon, dragging the grade column into rows and the answer column into values, and the counts appeared like magic. But every single question had the same winner: eighth grade. Pizza, eighth grade. Longer recess, eighth grade. Even "would you rather have a snow day or a field trip," eighth grade.

She frowned at the numbers. Something felt wrong. She remembered the assemblies in the gym, how the eighth graders filled whole bleacher rows while the sixth graders squeezed into one corner. She could deduce the problem from that memory alone: the eighth grade simply had more students, so of course their counts were bigger everywhere. She dragged "grade" into columns too and stared at the grid, but the raw counts still made eighth grade look like it won every argument.

Her brother Owen flopped onto the couch above her, chewing the end of a pen. "Did I win pizza?" he asked.

"Nobody wins yet," Brooke said. "The eighth graders just outnumber everybody. It's like weighing the sixth grade with plumbing pipes on the scale." Owen looked blank, so she waved a hand and went back to clicking.

She right-clicked a value in the table and noticed a menu called Show Values As. Her eye caught one option that said "% of Column Total," and she tried it, half expecting it to break everything. Instead every number turned into a percentage of its column total. Now the grades could actually be compared fairly, because each one showed its share of its own column rather than a raw count. The table rearranged itself in her head at the same time as on the screen. Sixth grade, it turned out, loved pizza at ninety-two percent, while eighth grade sat at only sixty-one. For snow days, seventh grade was the fanatic grade, not eighth at all. She laughed out loud, and Owen leaned over the couch arm to see.

"That's not fair," he said. "You said eighth won everything."

"I was wrong," Brooke said. "Raw counts fooled me." She thought about all the times she had decided something was true just because it was loud and frequent, like the kids who said nobody liked the school plays even though the quiet ones bought tickets every year. She left that thought unresolved, hovering, and started a fresh slide for Owen's report.

At the top she typed, in her most official font, "The Real Winners, by Percentage."

Jaxon crouched at the end of the hallway with a marble in one hand and his phone stopwatch in the other. His science teacher had assigned a lab on measuring speed, and Jaxon wanted the best graph in the class, but the hallway floor sloped in ways he couldn't see, and every measurement came out wrong unless he could figure out where the slope began. He laid a tape measure along the floorboards, marked off every meter with strips of masking tape, and decided to test his idea: if the ball crossed the marks faster and faster, the floor was tilted somewhere, even if nothing looked tilted.

His little sister Kayla came out of her room holding a folded note. "Don't open it until the race," she said, and pointed at the two marbles in his tray, a blue one and a green one. "I want the green one to be mine. We raced in the kitchen and I won, but you said I cheated because the table was slanted. So prove it here. You have to be impartial, Jaxon. No favoring your own marble." She set the green marble on the last strip of tape like it was a racehorse at a gate.

Jaxon ran each marble down the hallway five times, calling out the seconds while Kayla wrote the distances on a clipboard. Their dad passed through on his way to the kitchen, where he was stuffing sausage casings, and Jaxon glanced at the packet on the counter. "Real intestine," his dad said, tapping it. "Old-fashioned casing. Doesn't affect your marbles." He watched for a moment, then quietly brought a chair from the dining room so Kayla could sit while she wrote, because her knee had been bothering her all week.

Back in his room, Jaxon plotted the numbers. Time went across the bottom of his graph paper, distance went up the side, and each marble's points made a line. The blue line rose slowly and then bent upward, climbing steeper and steeper. The green line rose the same amount the whole way, steady as a staircase. He leaned close. The steep part of the blue line meant the blue marble was going faster there, while the flat green line meant it never sped up. He checked the stopwatch numbers again, and they matched. The steepness wasn't hiding anything anymore; it showed the speed plainly, the way the bend revealed the hidden slope his eyes had tried to conceal from him.

"So who won?" Kayla asked from the doorway. She was still holding her folded note.

"In the kitchen, your green marble won," Jaxon said, turning the graph toward her. "Look, the blue one's line here is steeper, and a steeper line means a faster speed. But only after the halfway point. Before that, your line is steeper. So you won the first half fair and square."

Kayla opened her note. In round pencil letters it said: If I really won, I get to pick the movie tonight. She held it up, grinning, and Jaxon laughed and reached for the remote.

Tyler had been staring at the same screen for twenty minutes, and the heading still sat stubbornly in the top left corner. "It's supposed to be centred," he said. "I put the rule in the CSS file. text-align: center. I checked the spelling three times."

Marcus rolled backward on his desk chair and peered over Tyler's shoulder. The basement smelled like dust and old carpet, and Marcus's gecko, Rocky, watched them from his tank on the shelf, blinking like he knew something they didn't. "The page is about Rocky, so it has to look good. My cousin Nadia is coming over at four, and she designs websites for actual money. She's going to demolish it if it looks like a potato made it."

"Thanks for the support."

"Focus. Did you refresh the browser?"

Tyler clicked refresh. Nothing. The big green heading that said ROCKY: THE MIGHTY CARNIVORE stayed exactly where it was, jammed against the left edge like it was trying to escape the page. He had spent all morning building the page itself, the HTML with its heading and paragraphs about crickets and mealworms, and Marcus had promised that style.css would make everything beautiful. It had made nothing beautiful. It had made nothing anything.

Tyler opened style.css again. The rule was there, plain as anything. He opened index.html. The heading was there. Two files, sitting in the same folder, ignoring each other completely. "It's like they've never met," he muttered.

"Maybe the file's broken," Marcus said. "Copy the rule into a different file and try that."

So Tyler created style2.css, typed the same rule, refreshed. Still nothing. His stomach tightened. Four o'clock was forty minutes away. He sat very still and thought about it the way he thought about math problems, looking for the thing he couldn't see. Two files in the same folder. One of them didn't know the other existed. The page didn't act like the CSS was wrong. It acted like the CSS wasn't there at all. Which meant the page had never been told about it.

"Marcus, how does a page find the stylesheet? Is there some kind of instruction?"

Marcus squinted at the ceiling. "Nadia said something about that once. She called it a link tag."

Tyler scrolled to the top of index.html, into the head section, and typed it out carefully: a link tag with rel="stylesheet" pointing to style.css. He saved, held his breath, and refreshed.

The heading glided to the exact centre of the page, green and enormous and perfect.

From the top of the stairs, a voice called down. "Hey, I'm early! Whatcha guys building?"

It was Nadia, and Marcus went pale. "Nothing," he called back. "Just a school thing."

She was already on the steps, and the first thing her eyes landed on was the screen. "Wait. Who centred that heading?"

"Tyler did," Marcus said quickly. "All by himself."

Tyler grinned. "I had an influential teacher."

Nadia frowned. "I didn't teach you anything yet."

The indoor track circled the hockey rink like a balcony, four laps to a mile, but Coach Ruiz wanted them ready for the outdoor season. He had taped a sign above the skate rental counter: remember, the outdoor track is 400 metres, so the 800 is exactly two laps, first lap and second lap. Charlie read it while she laced her shoes and watched the zamboni crawl below, flooding the ice for the little kids' practice.

Her problem was simple and stubborn. Every time she raced the 800, she exploded off the line, flew the first lap, and then her legs turned to sand for the second one, and girls she had beaten at the halfway point came past her one by one. Her friend Dana had texted her that morning: "You don't lose the race in the second lap. You lose it in the first. Try running the first lap like it's the boring half." Charlie had stared at the message on the bus, then at the fogged rink windows, and decided to test it.

"Two laps out there is the equivalent of eight laps up here," Dana said as they climbed to the track, breath steaming. "So run your first four up here slow on purpose, and see what's left."

Charlie regulated her breathing the way she'd practiced, counted her laps, and held herself back even when a boy from the speed-skating group surged past her. Her legs felt strange, almost lazy. On the fifth lap, she picked it up, and on the eighth she still had something left, enough to pass two skaters who had gone out too fast. One of them, a tall girl named Priya, sprinted at the end of lap six, arms pumping, face fierce, and then stumbled to a confused stop when Dana called, "That's not the finish! Two laps means the whole thing!" Priya had kicked a lap early and spent everything she had.

Afterward Charlie found Priya on the bleachers, unlacing her skates, eyes red. "I thought it was over," Priya said. "I was winning."

"You were," Charlie said. She sat down beside her. "That's the whole trick, I think. The race is longer than it feels." Then she took out her phone and typed a message to Dana: "It worked. First lap boring, second lap I actually had legs. But Priya kicked early and lost everything, and I feel bad about passing her." She looked down at the rink, where the little kids were wobbling onto the fresh ice, one small goalie already flat on his back, stick in the air, laughing.

Dana's reply buzzed in her hand: "That's the economy of racing. You spend where it counts. Some people learn it the easy way."

Charlie watched the goalie struggle up, fall again, and get up anyway.

Blake had been staring at the same line of code for ten minutes, and the line was winning. "It says nine is prime," he told Devon, turning the laptop so Devon could see the screen from his beanbag chair.

"Nine is three times three," Devon said around a mouthful of pretzels. "Your program is broken."

"I know it's broken. I just can't see why." Blake scrolled up through the file. The program was supposed to ask for a number, then run a loop from two up to that number, checking whether anything divided it evenly. Somewhere in that loop, his logic had turned obstinate and refused to catch nine. The problem was that division left no fingerprints. He couldn't watch it happen; he could only see the wrong answer it left behind.

"Print what the loop is doing," Devon suggested. "Make it show you."

Blake added a print statement inside the loop so the program would announce every number it tested. He ran it again, typed nine, and watched the lines scroll past. Two, three, four. At three, something odd happened: the check for divisibility printed true, but the program kept going and printed "prime" anyway. "There," Blake said, tapping the screen. "It found the factor and then ignored it. I bet my if statement isn't actually stopping anything."

He traced the indenting with his finger and found the print statement for "prime" sitting outside the loop, at the wrong level, so it ran no matter what the loop had discovered. One tab key, one deletion, and the fix was in. He typed nine again and the program said "not prime." He typed seven. Prime. Eleven. Prime.

"But how do we know it's right?" Devon asked. "We can't check a hundred numbers in our heads."

Blake looked around the basement. Devon's little sister, the household's most dedicated consumer of graph paper, had left a pad and pencils by the couch. Blake tore off a sheet and wrote the numbers one through fifty in rows. Then he started crossing out. He circled two and crossed out every second number after it. He circled three and crossed out every third number. Six was already gone, so he skipped it and kept going through the multiples.

"What are you doing?" Devon asked, leaning over his shoulder.

"It's called the Sieve of Eratosthenes," Blake said. "You cross out the multiples of each prime in turn. Whatever survives is prime."

They made the grid together, arguing only once, about whether forty-one deserved a circle. Then Blake ran his program on every survivor up to fifty, typing each number while Devon held the pencil over the grid like a judge. Forty-nine matched, and then Blake's fingers hovered over the keyboard for number fifty, the last one.

"Type it," Devon said. "No pressure."

The sugar had not moved in two minutes, and Thomas crouched over the camp stove like it might bolt if he looked away. He was making caramel for the birthday dessert, since the ice cream had turned to soup somewhere on the hike in and his little sister Priya had nearly ceased speaking to anyone over the loss. The plan was simple: pour the caramel over sliced peaches, sing the song, save the evening. The sugar was another matter. It sat in the pan, white and stubborn, while the first batch had burned to something that smelled like a campfire gone wrong.

"Your crust on the roast was brown," Priya said, watching over his shoulder. "Is that the same thing? Just sugar burning?"

Thomas thought about that. The roast had browned where the meat was, and there was no sugar on it at all, just salt and pepper. And the bread his grandfather baked every Sunday, that brown crust, no sugar in that dough either. So the browning could not be the same. "This is caramelization," he said. "Browning that happens when sugar alone gets heated. The crust on the roast is the Maillard reaction. That one needs amino acids too, so it's a different reaction."

"What are amino acids?"

"Protein stuff. Meat's full of it." He nudged the pan. "Sugar's just sugar."

Priya considered this with the seriousness of a judge. "So if I sprinkled sugar on the roast, would it be both?"

"Maybe don't experiment on Dad's birthday dinner."

The second batch of sugar finally began to melt at the edges, going clear, then gold. Thomas kept the flame low and swirled the pan, remembering how fast white had turned to charcoal last time. His family had a small dynasty of bad camp cooks, starting with his grandfather, who once served spaghetti that was still hard in the middle, and his father, who had already declared this trip's dinners "an endangered tradition." Thomas intended to be the one who changed that. He had one more cup of sugar and one chance.

Gold deepened to amber. He pulled the pan off the heat the second it looked right, added a knob of butter, and stirred until the bubbling calmed. The caramel poured over the peaches in a ribbon, glossy and smelling like everything good that had ever happened at a campfire.

"It's the same color as the roast," Priya observed, scooping her bowl.

"Same color, different reaction," Thomas said.

His father took a bite, then another, and held up his spoon like a man surrendering. "The dynasty," he said, "ends tonight."

Priya raised her bowl of peaches in salute, caramel dripping off her spoon onto the picnic table, where she cheerfully scraped it up with her finger.

The desk had someone else's initials carved into the corner, and Piper ran her thumb over them as the teacher read the seating chart. Room 114, Maple Ridge Middle School, third day of eighth grade. She had inherited the desk from a kid who had apparently needed to announce his existence with a pencil, and she had inherited the seat between two girls who were already whispering to each other.

At lunch she found the table with the fewest people, which was the table where Marisol sat alone, drawing in a notebook with a broken spiral. Piper set down her tray.

"Is this seat taken?"

"Nobody fights over it," Marisol said.

They talked about the art teacher's rule against paint in the hallways, which Marisol called rebellious nonsense, and Piper laughed once, for real. Afterward, walking to fifth period, Piper caught herself thinking they were friends now. Then she stopped on the stairs. That felt wrong, and she wanted to know why.

That night she searched on her phone, typing carefully, and found it: a 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas. It took about fifty hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Fifty hours. She did the math on the back of a permission slip. Lunch at Maple Ridge was twenty-two minutes. Even if she sat with Marisol every single day, that was under two hours a week. Fifty hours meant something like a whole semester of lunches, minimum, and probably longer, because nobody's school actually gave you a full twenty-two minutes of talking.

The next morning she started a tally in the margin of her science folder. One hash mark per lunch, and underneath, an estimate of minutes. On Thursday Marisol leaned over and squinted at it.

"What is that?"

"Data," Piper said. "A study in 2018, by Jeffrey Hall at the University of Kansas, found it takes about fifty hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. I'm testing it."

"On me?"

"On us." Piper held her breath.

Marisol tapped the page twice, thinking. "Then you're wasting minutes in study hall sitting alone." She pulled out a pen and added a hash mark of her own, slightly crooked. "Also, my brother has strep. He's on that pink antibiotic, the one that tastes like chalk, and Mom says he'll be home all weekend being miserable at me."

"So you need somewhere to be."

"I'm just saying. Saturday. Hours count double when there's a sick brother involved."

Piper looked at the tally, then at the crooked mark, then at Marisol's pen still hovering over the paper.

"Saturday," she said, and drew the next line herself.

The basement smelled like popcorn and old carpet, and the only light came from Dario's laptop and a string of mismatched bulbs his dad had wired along the ceiling. Asher pulled his chair closer. He had one goal tonight: finish the prime checker before his mom picked him up at eight.

"Type it exactly like this," Dario said, sliding the laptop over. "A loop that tries every number up to the one you pick."

Asher wrote the program line by line, his fingers slow on the unfamiliar keys. Ask for a number, then divide it by everything smaller, and print whether it was prime. It felt strange, like the laptop was a conductor and his code was the current, invisible until it did something wrong. He ran it and typed 9.

The screen filled with text. Not prime. Not prime. Not prime. Line after line scrolled past, dozens of them, the fan whirring like the machine was annoyed.

"Why is it saying it nine times?" Asher asked.

"Because your loop keeps going," Dario said. He leaned back in his chair, which squeaked on the concrete floor. "It found a divisor, but it didn't stop."

Asher stared at the wall of words. Somewhere in his program, the computer already knew the answer, and it was still marching on anyway, checking every number left like someone who'd found their keys and kept searching the couch. He scrolled up through his code, tapping the trackpad. There had to be a way to quit early.

He tried putting the word break inside his loop, right after the print. When he ran it again and typed 9, the screen showed Not prime exactly once. He typed 13 and got prime. He tried 25, 31, 49. One line each time.

"That's it," he said, grinning. "A break statement stops a loop immediately." Dario laughed and gave him a fist bump, and they split the last of the popcorn while the program waited for another number.

Later, while Dario went upstairs for sodas, Asher found a note taped to the monitor, in Dario's eccentric handwriting, all loops and slants. "Don't insulate yourself from the weird error messages," it read. "They're how the machine talks. Read every one."

Asher pulled out his phone and opened a message to his cousin Priya, who wanted the program for her math club. I got it working, he typed. Want me to show you how tomorrow? He set the phone down and looked at the blinking cursor on the dark screen, waiting for the next number someone would type.

"Dario," he called toward the stairs, "what's the biggest number you know?"

The bank had set up a table in the mall between the pretzel stand and the fountain, and a folding sign promised five percent on a teen savings account. Lydia stopped because her mother was still in the shoe store, and because two hundred forty dollars, her entire fortune from two summers of dog walking, was sitting at home in a jar.

"With simple interest," the woman at the table said, "five percent of your money gets added every year. Two hundred forty dollars, five percent, that's twelve dollars a year."

Lydia did the math in her head. Twelve dollars times five years was sixty dollars, so three hundred at the end. Then the woman slid a brochure across the table. "Or there's the compound account. Interest earns interest there."

Lydia borrowed the calculator chained to the table. She typed 240 times 1.05, and it said 252. Fine. But a year later it wouldn't be 240 earning interest, it would be 252, so she typed 1.05 again, and got 264.60. She kept multiplying by 1.05 until she'd done it five times. 306.30. With compound interest, her money at graduation would be 306 dollars and 30 cents, not 300. Six dollars and thirty cents more, just for letting the interest pile up on itself. She found the little power key with the y to the x on it and tried 240 times 1.05 to the fifth, and it came out the same, 306.30, which felt like a magic trick she had performed for herself.

"So the compound one wins," she said.

"Over five years, a little," the woman said. "Over twenty, you'd notice."

A man with a stroller tried to get past the table, and the sign obstructed his path until Lydia shifted it. The woman apologized and mentioned the bank was a tenant of the mall, like everybody else with a table or a shop, and Lydia filed that away as a fact she would never need.

The trouble was the fine print. Compound account, five dollars a month maintenance fee. Lydia stood at the fountain and did it again: sixty dollars in fees over five years, against six dollars and thirty cents in extra interest. The dog-walking money would be better off in the jar, if the jar earned nothing at all. She walked back to the shoe store feeling oddly optimistic, the way you do when a bad deal fails to fool you.

"Mom," she said, holding out the brochure, "we need to talk about my retirement."
